intro: This is the last unit of the course, and it turns outward and then back in. First it follows the Bible out of the synagogue and the church into the wider world. You will meet Milton's epic and Morrison's novels, the Sistine ceiling and Handel's Messiah. You will hear the spirituals, the sermons of 1860 and Lincoln's answer in 1865. You will read the speeches of Frederick Douglass and Martin Luther King Jr. And you will study the Supreme Court cases that explain why a public school can study this book at all. At every stop you will ask what a reader kept, what a reader changed, and what a reader's own moment supplied.

Then it asks you to do the work yourself. The capstone is a close reading of one passage, argued from the text. You will choose it with care and read it in two translations. You will map its genre and shape, trace its key words, and set it in its world. You will check it against Jewish, Christian and academic readers. Then you will write a thesis about what the passage does and means, support it with citations, and state the readings you do not adopt in their strongest form. You will deliver the argument twice: as an essay and as a short presentation with the text open.

By the end you will be able to trace a verse through a culture. You will be able to argue about a passage with evidence and attribute every belief to the people who hold it. You will be able to read a sacred text in a room full of people who read it differently. Those are skills for the rest of your life. This book turns up in courts, museums, elections and conversations, and you will know how to read it when it does.
bigQuestion: How has the Bible shaped the culture around you, and how do you read one of its passages closely, fairly and with an argument of your own?

timeline.t: John Winthrop tells Puritan settlers they will be as a city upon a hill (Matthew 5:14)
Milton publishes Paradise Lost, retelling Genesis 2–3 in ten books, revised to twelve in 1674
Bunyan publishes The Pilgrim's Progress, an allegory built from Bible verses
Handel's Messiah, with words from the King James Bible, is first performed in Dublin
Frederick Douglass publishes his Narrative, contrasting two Christianities
Melville publishes Moby-Dick, with Ishmael, Ahab and a sermon on Jonah
Lincoln's Second Inaugural: both sides read the same Bible and pray to the same God
The Fisk Jubilee Singers begin touring, bringing spirituals to concert halls
McCollum v. Board of Education, from Champaign, Illinois, ends religious instruction in public school buildings
Abington v. Schempp permits objective study of the Bible in public schools; King's 'I Have a Dream' echoes Amos and Isaiah
Toni Morrison publishes Beloved, with an epigraph from Romans 9:25
You choose a passage, read it in two translations, consult three readers and argue from the text

words.d: the history of how a text has been read, retold, painted, sung or argued over after it was written
a story whose characters, places and events stand for ideas, such as The Pilgrim's Progress
a short quotation placed at the start of a book to set its theme
a large musical work for singers and orchestra on a sacred subject, such as Handel's Messiah
a religious song created by enslaved African Americans, often drawing on Exodus and the prophets
reading later people or events as repeating a biblical pattern
the part of the First Amendment that forbids government from establishing religion
a self-contained unit of text, such as a parable, psalm or scene
a translation approach that follows the words and order of the original closely
a Hebrew word for loyal love or faithful kindness, central to the book of Ruth
the one-sentence claim an essay argues for; in a capstone, a claim about what the text does and means
stating a view you do not hold in its strongest form before responding to it

test.q: What does reception mean in the study of the Bible?
choices: The history of how a text has been read, retold and reused
The reading of Torah in a synagogue
test.why: Reception study follows a text into later poems, paintings, songs and arguments.

test.q: Which detail comes from Milton rather than from Genesis 3?
choices: A tree in the middle of the garden
Satan's speech about envy before entering the serpent
test.why: Genesis names only the serpent; Satan's speeches are Paradise Lost.

test.q: Who compiled the King James verses that Handel set in Messiah?
test.why: Jennens assembled the libretto in 1741; Handel wrote the music.

test.q: Which passage did abolitionists cite against slavery?
choices: Exodus 21:16, on stealing and selling a person
test.why: Exodus 21:16 makes kidnapping a capital crime; the other three were cited by defenders of slavery.

test.q: What did Lincoln say about the Bible in his Second Inaugural?
choices: Only the North read it rightly
It should be kept out of politics
Both sides read the same Bible and prayed to the same God
test.why: Lincoln refused to claim God for either side and quoted Matthew 18:7 and Psalm 19:9.

test.q: Which prophet's call for justice to roll down like waters did King draw on in 1963?
test.why: King echoed Amos 5:24, along with Isaiah 40:4–5.

test.q: What did Abington v. Schempp (1963) decide?
choices: Public schools must read the Bible each morning
Public schools may not mention religion
Only private schools may teach about the Bible
Public schools may not hold devotional Bible reading but may study the Bible objectively
test.why: Justice Clark's opinion drew the line between religious exercise and academic study.

test.q: Which Supreme Court case came from Champaign, Illinois?
test.why: McCollum (1948) ended religious instruction inside Champaign's public schools.

choices: A commentary printed beside the text
A self-contained unit of text such as a parable or psalm
test.why: A pericope is the unit the text itself marks off, the right size for a capstone.

test.q: Which pair of translations may be quoted freely in a capstone?
choices: King James Version and JPS Tanakh 1917
test.why: The KJV and JPS 1917 are public domain; modern versions are copyrighted and should be paraphrased.

test.q: How does the King James Version translate hesed in Ruth?
test.why: Kindness appears in Ruth 1:8, 2:20 and 3:10; the word is mercy in Psalm 23:6.

test.q: How should a capstone present a Christian reading of Ruth through Matthew 1:5?
choices: As a Christian reading, attributed and stated in its own terms
As the same as Rashi's reading
test.why: Every reading is attributed and described as its readers would recognize it.

test.q: Which sentence is a workable capstone thesis?
choices: Ruth proves that God rewards loyalty
Ruth's speech is the book's first act of hesed, against which every other character is measured
test.why: It claims something specific about what the text does that can be tested against the words; the others are a reaction, a claim about God and an overconfident date.

choices: Stating a view you do not hold in its strongest form before responding
test.why: The capstone presents other readings so their holders would recognize them, then responds.

test.q: What does objectivity mean for studying the Bible in a public school?
choices: Describing the text and its readings accurately without adopting or dismissing any
Pretending the text has no religious weight
test.why: Schempp permits objective study, which the course defines as accurate, attributed description.

write.prompt: Choose one passage from this course and one later use of it, such as Handel's Isaiah 40, King's Amos 5:24, Winthrop's Matthew 5:14 or Morrison's Romans 9:25. Cite the passage by book, chapter and verse in a named translation. Explain what the passage says in its own setting, how Jewish and Christian readers have read it, and what the later user kept, changed and supplied.
tips: Quote the passage from a public-domain translation and name it, or paraphrase a modern one with a citation.
Attribute every belief: 'Christians read this as', 'Jewish tradition hears', 'many scholars think'.
Compare the readings to the text and to each other, never to the truth.
Use the unit's terms: reception, setting, typology, thesis, attribution.
Say what the later use changed, and do not call it a mistake; say what it did and why.
